# The Swatch Group AG (UHR.SW) — Forensic Dossier

*Bearer share, listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange, priced in Swiss francs (CHF). All per-share figures are per bearer share (~51.9 million bearer-equivalent shares outstanding). Swatch reports twice a year and does not hold quarterly earnings calls, so no earnings-call transcript exists for this name; this dossier cross-references the published half-year and full-year results, management's written outlook, and the public record of the 2025–2026 shareholder fight against the hard financial trajectory from our screener.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story here is a three-act cyclical collapse, not a growth story. Coming out of 2021–2023, Swatch rode the post-pandemic luxury boom: revenue climbed from CHF 5.6 billion (2020) to a peak of CHF 7.89 billion (2023), and net profit reached CHF 869 million. Management's language in that window was offensive — capacity investment, new movements, Chinese demand recovery.

Act two was the China luxury bust. In 2024 revenue fell to CHF 6.74 billion and net profit collapsed 78% to CHF 219 million as Greater China (roughly a third of sales) went into a deep spending recession. By full-year 2025 the picture was worse on the bottom line even as the top line stabilized: revenue CHF 6.28 billion (down only about 1.3% at constant exchange rates, better than the roughly 4% decline feared), but net profit essentially evaporated to CHF 25 million and operating margin fell to about 2.1%. The core problem migrated from demand to under-absorption: Swatch is heavily vertically integrated (it makes its own movements through ETA and hairsprings through Nivarox and supplies much of the Swiss industry), so when volumes drop, its factories carry large fixed-cost losses.

Act three, now underway, is management's "recovery" chapter. The first-half 2026 report (published end of June 2026) showed sales up 8.5% at constant exchange rates to CHF 3.12 billion, with the core Watches & Jewelry division up 9.5% and its operating margin climbing to about 15% in May and June. Management's stated 2026 outlook is unusually bold: "substantial growth" across all price segments that will "massively reduce, or even help reverse" the production losses and materially improve group profitability.

The single most important narrative thread the numbers force us to hold, though, runs alongside the operating story: a two-year governance battle. Steven Wood of GreenWood Investors has campaigned since 2025 for a board seat to represent minority (bearer) shareholders and to push a sharper luxury focus and better capital allocation. He was rejected a second time in May 2026, with 79.6% of votes cast against him — the Hayek family used its roughly 44% voting control to block him. This is the load-bearing fact for anyone underwriting the discount to book value.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The financial evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Substantial growth in 2026, massively reduced production losses" | H1 2026 sales +8.5% at constant FX; Watches & Jewelry margin reached ~15% in May–June. But reported operating profit still *fell* to CHF 52M (1.7% margin) from CHF 68M, and net profit fell ~88% | Directionally supported at constant currency; contradicted at the reported level by a ~CHF 200M franc-strength headwind |
| Demand is recovering, China stabilizing | China (incl. HK/Macau) retail sales +9% in H1 2026 with stable point-of-sale count; third-party replenishment still "modest" | Genuine improvement, but sell-through is ahead of wholesale — retailers are not yet restocking |
| The brands remain premium | Gross margin still ~82% (5.16B on 6.28B in 2025) | Confirmed — pricing power at the product level is intact; the collapse is in operating leverage, not brand value |
| Balance sheet is a fortress | Net liquidity ~CHF 1.1–1.2B, equity ratio ~87%, near-zero debt (CHF 236M) against CHF 11.4B equity | Confirmed and central to the thesis |
| Capital discipline | Inventory held at CHF 7.3B — over 1,000 days of sales — and dividend maintained at CHF 4.50/bearer share despite near-zero profit; no buyback despite the stock at ~0.82x book | The number that most damages the "shareholder-friendly" claim: capital is trapped in inventory the family will not monetize, and buybacks at a deep discount are declined |

Where the story is *richer* than the numbers: the reported P&L. Constant-currency momentum is real, but the strong Swiss franc is quietly eating most of it, so an investor buying "the recovery" is also implicitly taking a currency view. Where the story is *poorer* than the numbers: the balance sheet is genuinely stronger than a 2% margin suggests — CHF 149/share of net current assets sits behind a CHF 180 share.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising, from a low base.** Through 2024 the tone was defensive — cost, China, "difficult environment." The January 2026 full-year commentary and the mid-2026 half-year report shifted decisively to offensive language ("substantial growth," "very positive volume developments," margin recovery quantified month-by-month). CEO Nick Hayek has consistently framed the downturn as cyclical and self-correcting rather than structural, and he has consistently declined to change strategy (no buybacks, no brand disposals, no board opening). Confidence is rising; flexibility is not.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium.** The screener's own record — beat 1 of 8 quarters (12%) — and a five-year EPS trajectory from CHF 16.76 (2023) to near zero (2025) tell you management's optimism has repeatedly run ahead of delivery through the downturn. The credit side: full-year 2025 constant-currency sales came in better than feared, and the 2026 half-year confirmed the top-line inflection they promised. So the *sales* guidance is tracking; the *profit* guidance ("massively improved profitability") has yet to show up in the reported operating line because currency and factory under-absorption are still absorbing the gains. Reliability on volumes is improving; reliability on margins is unproven.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The recurring, unanswered questions are governance and capital allocation, not operations. Analysts and the activist have pressed on: why hold CHF 7.3B of inventory rather than shrink it and buy back deeply discounted stock; why maintain a dual-class structure that lets a 44%-voting family override the 75% of economic capital held by outside investors; why decline a minority-representative board seat that even ISS supported. Management's answer has been to defend "capacity and the dividend" and to disqualify the activist candidate on nationality and a conflicting board seat. The gap between what outside holders want (value realization) and what the family will permit is the central, unresolved tension.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Operating margin collapsed from ~15–18% (mid-cycle) to ~2%; ROIC of about 0.2% (trailing twelve months) is far below the cost of capital.
🔴 Reported profit still falling (net profit −88% in H1 2026) despite constant-currency sales growth — the franc is a persistent, uncontrollable headwind.
🔴 Governance is family-captured; the activist value-unlock path was rejected twice, most recently May 2026 (79.6% against).
🔴 Capital trapped: CHF 7.3B inventory (>1,000 days), no buyback at 0.82x book.
🟢 Fortress balance sheet: ~CHF 1.1B net cash, 87% equity ratio, negligible debt.
🟢 Gross margin intact at ~82% — the brands themselves are not impaired.
🟢 Genuine, dated top-line inflection: H1 2026 sales +8.5% constant FX, China retail +9%, Watches & Jewelry margin to ~15% in May–June.
🟢 Dividend maintained (CHF 4.50/bearer) through the trough — a signal of family confidence in the recovery.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling shift is what management chose to disclose in H1 2026: a *monthly* margin path (Watches & Jewelry hitting ~15% in May and June). Breaking out intra-half-year margin acceleration is a deliberate confidence signal — it invites you to annualize the exit rate rather than the average. Read skeptically, it is also an admission that the reported half-year average margin was still poor. Second, the persistence of "modest" third-party replenishment tells you the channel is not yet convinced; the recovery is retail sell-through led, which is the healthier but slower path. Third, the dividend-over-buyback choice, repeated again in 2026, quietly confirms the family will return cash on *its* terms (a flat payout to all shareholders including itself) rather than the terms minorities would choose (repurchasing stock below book).

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABILIZING / early-cyclical-turn, inside a permanently family-controlled structure.** The business is troughing and turning at the top line, the balance sheet is unimpeachable, and the brands retain full pricing power. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is a real, cheap-on-assets franchise whose value the controlling family has twice refused to let outsiders unlock, so the discount to book is structural, not a countdown to a catalyst.** You are buying a cyclical earnings recovery at roughly book value, not a value-realization event.

**Moat:** intangible-brand plus vertical-integration/scale-cost (ETA/Nivarox supply the industry). It is a **narrow** moat in practice — Swatch earns structurally lower returns than Richemont or LVMH even at peak, and its mid-market brands (Swatch, Tissot, Certina) sit in the price band most exposed to smartwatch substitution. **Trend: stable/troughing** — gross margin is holding at ~82% and volumes are turning up, so the moat is not structurally eroding; the ROIC collapse is cyclical under-absorption plus currency, not brand decay. **Secular threat: manageable** — the smartwatch pressures the low end, but luxury mechanical watches (Omega, Breguet, Blancpain, Longines) endure as status goods; the durable drag on *shareholder* value is governance, not a secular force impairing terminal brand value. The cheapness is therefore a genuine cyclical fear-print on the assets, but one gated by a family that will not convert the discount into cash for minorities.

The gap between what outside holders want (value realization) and what the family will permit is the central, unresolved tension.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Operating margin collapsed from ~15–18% (mid-cycle) to ~2%; ROIC of about 0.2% (trailing twelve months) is far below the cost of capital.
🔴 Reported profit still falling (net profit −88% in H1 2026) despite constant-currency sales growth — the franc is a persistent, uncontrollable headwind.
🔴 Governance is family-captured; the activist value-unlock path was rejected twice, most recently May 2026 (79.6% against).
🔴 Capital trapped: CHF 7.3B inventory (>1,000 days), no buyback at 0.82x book.
🟢 Fortress balance sheet: ~CHF 1.1B net cash, 87% equity ratio, negligible debt.
🟢 Gross margin intact at ~82% — the brands themselves are not impaired.
🟢 Genuine, dated top-line inflection: H1 2026 sales +8.5% constant FX, China retail +9%, Watches & Jewelry margin to ~15% in May–June.
🟢 Dividend maintained (CHF 4.50/bearer) through the trough — a signal of family confidence in the recovery.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling shift is what management chose to disclose in H1 2026: a *monthly* margin path (Watches & Jewelry hitting ~15% in May and June). Breaking out intra-half-year margin acceleration is a deliberate confidence signal — it invites you to annualize the exit rate rather than the average. Read skeptically, it is also an admission that the reported half-year average margin was still poor. Second, the persistence of "modest" third-party replenishment tells you the channel is not yet convinced; the recovery is retail sell-through led, which is the healthier but slower path. Third, the dividend-over-buyback choice, repeated again in 2026, quietly confirms the family will return cash on *its* terms (a flat payout to all shareholders including itself) rather than the terms minorities would choose (repurchasing stock below book).

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABILIZING / early-cyclical-turn, inside a permanently family-controlled structure.** The business is troughing and turning at the top line, the balance sheet is unimpeachable, and the brands retain full pricing power. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is a real, cheap-on-assets franchise whose value the controlling family has twice refused to let outsiders unlock, so the discount to book is structural, not a countdown to a catalyst.** You are buying a cyclical earnings recovery at roughly book value, not a value-realization event.

**Moat:** intangible-brand plus vertical-integration/scale-cost (ETA/Nivarox supply the industry). It is a **narrow** moat in practice — Swatch earns structurally lower returns than Richemont or LVMH even at peak, and its mid-market brands (Swatch, Tissot, Certina) sit in the price band most exposed to smartwatch substitution. **Trend: stable/troughing** — gross margin is holding at ~82% and volumes are turning up, so the moat is not structurally eroding; the ROIC collapse is cyclical under-absorption plus currency, not brand decay. **Secular threat: manageable** — the smartwatch pressures the low end, but luxury mechanical watches (Omega, Breguet, Blancpain, Longines) endure as status goods; the durable drag on *shareholder* value is governance, not a secular force impairing terminal brand value. The cheapness is therefore a genuine cyclical fear-print on the assets, but one gated by a family that will not convert the discount into cash for minorities.
